prime.problem: A Transformer only reads integers. Something has to turn arbitrary text (any language, emoji, code) into a short list of ids, and the choice of how to chop the text decides what the model can and can't see.
prime.fits: The GPT lecture used the simplest tokenizer possible: one id per character, 65 in all. This card is the first of the tokenizer lecture; it shows why real models replace that with about 50,000 byte-level BPE chunks, and lists the failures the rest of the course will trace back to it.
expect: the tokenizer as a separate stage
prime.goal: Explain why GPT-2 tokenizes into byte-level BPE chunks instead of characters, code points or raw bytes, and predict which kinds of task that choice makes hard.

attend: Why did the vocabulary grow about 773 times from 65 to 50,257, while the Shakespeare sequence shrank only about 3.3 times?
What does the model receive for " Citizen", and what does it never get to see about that word?
Why does starting BPE from the 256 bytes mean no string can ever fail to encode?
Where does a bigger vocabulary cost you inside the model, and where does it save you?
Which of the listed symptoms come from hidden letters, and which from how the tokenizer's training data was chosen?

must: The model sees only token ids → the characters inside a token are invisible to it → tasks that need individual letters (spelling, counting l's, reversing) get hard
Chunks instead of characters → 3.30 characters per GPT-2 token on Shakespeare → the same 256-token window holds about 845 characters instead of 256 → more context for the same attention cost
Start from the 256 byte values, then merge frequent pairs → every string encodes (no unknown characters, unlike the 65-character vocab) → while common chunks stay short sequences

vocab_size sets the rows of the embedding table and the width of the output layer → 50,257 × 384 = 19,298,688 numbers vs 24,960 for 65 characters → a bigger vocab isn't free, and rare tokens' rows get little training
elevated: The tokenizer is trained separately, on its own text, before the LLM → which languages and formats get short tokens depends on that text → non-English text and odd formats cost more tokens (132 GPT-2 tokens for a 72-character Korean line)
reference: GPT-2 context length 1024 tokens (up from 512 in GPT-1)
the Colab's exact list of eleven symptom questions

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the path from a raw string to the model's output: text → tokenizer → ids → embedding table → Transformer → next-id probabilities. Then, in 3–4 sentences, say why GPT-2 uses byte-level BPE and what that choice hides from the model.
checklist: the model reads integers only; the tokenizer turns text into ids and back
the tokenizer is its own stage, trained once on its own text before the LLM
byte-level BPE: 256 byte tokens as the base, so any string encodes, plus 50,000 learned merges
chunks shorten sequences (3.30 characters per token on Shakespeare), so more text fits in the window
cost: letters inside a token are invisible, and a bigger vocab means a bigger embedding table and output layer

retrieve.q: Explain why a model that is excellent at writing English can still miscount the letters in a word it writes correctly.
answer: it reads and writes token ids, not letters
a common word or chunk is one id (e.g. "DefaultCellStyle" is 1 GPT-4 token)
the letter count is not visible in the id; the model has to have memorised it

retrieve.q: Walk "café" through the GPT lecture's character tokenizer and then through GPT-2's tokenizer. What happens in each?
answer: character tokenizer: stoi['é'] doesn't exist, so encode raises a KeyError
GPT-2: the text becomes UTF-8 bytes, so é is 2 bytes that always have tokens
merges then group it into 3 tokens: c, af, é

retrieve.q: You could give a model a 65-token, a 50,257-token or a 100,277-token vocabulary. What does moving up buy you, and what does it cost?
answer: buys shorter sequences: Shakespeare goes 1,115,394 → 338,025 → 301,829 tokens
so more text fits in a fixed context window
costs a bigger embedding table and output layer (24,960 → 19,298,688 → 38,506,368 numbers at n_embd 384)
and more rare tokens whose rows get little training

retrieve.q: Sort these into "hidden letters" vs "tokenizer training data" causes: bad spelling, bloated Korean, string reversal, SolidGoldMagikarp.
answer: hidden letters: spelling, reversal
training-data choice: Korean gets few merges so it costs more tokens
SolidGoldMagikarp: a token that was in the tokenizer's training text but almost never in the LLM's, so its row stayed untrained

compare.q: The GPT lecture's stoi/itos tokenizer vs GPT-2's byte-level BPE: what is fundamentally different about how each builds its vocabulary, and how does each one fail?
answer: characters: vocab = the distinct characters in the training text, no training step
BPE: 256 bytes plus merges learned from a separate training text
characters fail on any unseen character (KeyError) and give long sequences
BPE never fails to encode but hides letters and needs a big table; characters are the right pick for a tiny single-text demo

compare.q: Why not just use Unicode code points or raw UTF-8 bytes as tokens directly? What does each choice break, and how does BPE keep the good half of the bytes option?
answer: code points: over 130,000 base symbols and a standard that keeps changing
raw bytes: only 256 symbols, but sequences get longer than characters
BPE keeps the 256-byte base (any string encodes) and merges frequent byte runs to shorten sequences

predict.q: The GPT-2 tokenizer was trained on mostly English web text. You feed it a 72-character Korean line and a 76-character English line. Roughly how do their token counts compare, and why?
predict.answer: About 132 tokens for the Korean vs 20 for the English (measured with tiktoken). Korean characters are 3 UTF-8 bytes each, and the tokenizer's training text had little Korean, so few Korean byte runs got merged. The line's 158 bytes become 132 tokens, only 1.2 bytes per token on average. The model sees over 6 times as many tokens for the same length of text, so it fills its context faster. The tour card shows the same line in cl100k (61 tokens).

apply.task: Copy the Build-it script and add one line: print(len(enc.encode(text[:256*4]))), which tokenizes the first 1,024 characters of Shakespeare. Before running, predict the count from the card's 3.30 characters per token. Then encode "café" with both the GPT lecture's stoi and enc, and explain the difference.
apply.done: The script prints 292 (a 3.30-based guess of about 310 is within 10%), stoi raises a KeyError on é, and enc.encode("café") returns 3 ids.
apply.hint: 1,024 / 3.30 ≈ 310. The start of Shakespeare is mostly short dialogue lines and speaker names, so it can differ from the whole-file average.
